items.title: 66095_Benny Carter oral history interview
items.q: So I went out to Chicago, and Teddy Wilson was playing at this place... I talked to Teddy, and he finally consented to come to New York -- because I guess I had some recording dates... he realized that there might be more opportunity to further his career in New York

ctx.x: So, how did Teddy Wilson join -- it was this group that Teddy Wilson joined when he came to New York?

Yes, that was about 1933, when I had been playing with Fletcher sometime before then, we were playing a date in Providence, Rhode Island, and following that engagement that night, we had a night off. Roy Eldridge suggested we drive up to hear Speed Webb and Speed Webb had a very fine pianist that Roy thought I would like.
So we went up there, and I heard the pianist and I was just oh, tremendously impressed - and it was Teddy Wilson.

items.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: with the Benny Goodman Quartet there was no bass player... Teddy Wilson, who was one of the younger guys... I always had him in mind... John Hammond was trying to help me put the band together

ctx.x: Oh, Freddy Johnson, yes, I knew him. He lived on 99th Street. He didn’t live on San Juan Hill. Now, we got to play together quite a bit in those days, because one thing that I was always able to get were jobs in the dance halls, you know, the dime-a-dance places. Usually it was me, Freddy Johnson, and Walter Johnson, the drummer, because the trios at that time didn’t use bass players. You know, the pianists always, as I mentioned before, had a pretty sturdy left hand, and with the drummer, they just didn’t need a…

items.title: 66600_Teddy Wilson oral history interview
items.q: As a matter of fact, the Chocolate Dandies under Benny Carter -- two of the Chocolate Dandies were white when I did it

ctx.x: So Horace Henderson had a really great band in those days, and Benny Carter, right out of school, want too, in Ohio, they formed this great band, and Rex Steele was in that band -- so I heard this kind of music in my summer vacations in Detroit, and when I go back to Alabama to school, they would -- that impression was just so strong, see. So that was really why Detroit was the town I settled in, and joined the union, tried to start a career after I had left school.
